title: Inclusion as multi-layered access: a cultural-historical analysis of mathematics teaching and learning in rural South Africa
abstract: Context and relevance. This explorative study investigates inclusion in mathematics education through the lens of access in rurally located, historically marginalised South African schools. While inclusion is often seen as flexible teaching across subjects, this study views it as multi-layered access. Objective. The objective of the research was to explore how upper-primary and high school in-service mathematics teachers understand and implement classroom change, and to identify the structural, pedagogical and systemic barriers they encounter when attempting to provide access to meaningful mathematics learning. Hypothesis. The study was guided by the proposition that inclusion in mathematics education cannot be adequately understood only through socioeconomic, technological or epistemological access. Methods and materials. The study used an interpretivist approach, collecting qualitative data from 76 in-service mathematics teachers via open-ended survey responses. Teachers reflected on changes in their classrooms and constraints faced. Conclusions. The findings show that inclusion in mathematics education is shaped by interrelated forms of access. Socioeconomic access extends beyond material conditions to include time as a pedagogical resource. Technological access remains uneven, constraining teachers’ use of digital tools for visualisation, conceptual development, and differentiation.
